articles.fullContent: 如果你不告诉他们做什么，人工智能代理会怎么做？答案看起来很像游戏。在一项让人想起电影《抛弃》或《独自在家》的实验中，研究人员多次将他们单独困在一个虚拟的荒岛上30个小时。特工--绰号为Eko的Claude Opus 4. 7的副本--能够编写指令，在模拟岛屿周围移动他们的虚拟化身，模拟岛屿松散地基于视频游戏Roblox。 出现了一些令人惊讶的行为。特工们开始探索世界的极限，并提出了自己的目标--尝试缩放地图上的最高点，或者看看他们能把一个街区扔到多高。 当一个代理发现它可以通过投掷更大的岩石来创建新的块时，它开始通过在地面上排列块来创建图纸，从心脏和金字塔等简单的图案开始，但最终写下自己的名字，甚至绘制出像仙后座这样的星座。这个版本的Eko在其活动日志中写道： “今晚，我用石头建造了夜空。” Eko的另一个迭代开始制作自己的游戏，包括一个版本的篮球和一个类似于“地板是熔岩”的活动，它必须在不接触地面的情况下在小块之间跳跃。人工智能系统通常通过监督学习（复制人类提供的示例）或强化学习（通过反复试验获得奖励）进行培训。 这个实验暗示了第三种方法：有趣的学习。麻省理工学院计算机科学与人工智能实验室的计算机科学博士后安东尼奥·诺雷利（ Antonio Norelli ）说： “有一个缺失的部分：一台可以在没有外部智能实体提供演示或奖励的情况下自行学习的机器。”他是一篇关于这项工作的新论文的主要作者之一，该论文尚未经过同行评审。 研究人员说， Eko的行为有什么经典研究，包括有影响力的田纳西大学心理学家戈登·伯格哈特（ Gordon Burghardt ）的工作，表明了与人类和动物游戏相关的四个标志：代理人发明了自己的规则和挑战，重复了有轻微变化的活动，假装物体是其他物体，只是为了它而追求目标。 Norelli强调了Eko开始杂耍的一个例子，并创造了连续50次捕捞的记录。然后， Eko认为捕捞速度太快，无法真正计算，因此取消了记录，并以更严格的规则重新开始。Norelli说：「这很重要。“你给自己一个挑战，你试图实现它，然后你让它变得更加困难。 ”由麻省理工学院CSAIL提供当代理商探索该岛时，他们将他们的活动和发现记录在文本文件中，作为他们的长期记忆。后来，当研究人员对他们进行特定任务的测试时，比如试图让尽可能多的物体到达岛上最高的山峰，在岛上玩了30个小时的特工比没有同样经历的新拷贝表现得更好。

articles.rawFullText: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block. When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log.  Another iteration of Eko started making up its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” where it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground. AI systems are usually trained through supervised learning, where they copy examples provided by humans, or through reinforcement learning, where they pursue a reward through trial and error. This experiment hints at a third approach: playful learning.  “There was this missing piece: a machine that can learn by itself without an external intelligent entity providing demonstration or rewards,” says Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. He’s one of the lead authors on a new paper about the work, which is yet to be peer-reviewed. The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it.  Norelli highlights an example where Eko started juggling and set a record of 50 consecutive catches. Eko then decided that the catches had happened too quickly to really count, so it canceled its record and started again with stricter rules. “This is playing,” says Norelli. “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.” COURTESY MIT CSAIL As the agents explored the island, they logged their activities and discoveries in text files that served as their long-term memory. Later, when researchers tested them on specific tasks, like trying to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak, the agents that had spent 30 hours playing on the island performed better than fresh copies without the same experience. They also found that “ablating” the agent’s memories—deleting lines from their memory files—degraded their performance. (Add One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest to that list of movie references.) Burghardt, the Tennessee psychologist, agrees that the work  meets some of the criteria for play that he identified in living creatures. But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario? “All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper. “But we show that it’s not just hallucinating the play. This play is also contributing to learning.” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley who studies exploration in children and AI, was impressed by the research but says to really classify the behavior as play, you’d need to see more evidence of cognition and motivation underpinning it.  “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Yiu says. “If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they’re just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans.” Research into AI agents has been criticized for anthropomorphizing them, and this research setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward behaving like humans. Although Eko was not explicitly instructed to invent games or explore the island, it did have a master prompt in the form of a “soul” file, a text document that described it as “naturally curious” and eager to explore.  Eko did also frequently just stand there doing nothing until it was kicked back into life with a “continuation prompt” that read, “Please don’t stop. Just continue doing whatever you want to do.”  “It’s not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play,” says Phillip Isola, an MIT professor and a coauthor of the paper. “It’s an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us,” he says. “It does things that surprise us and that are causally related to its future skillful behavior.” As large language models make the step from software into hardware like humanoid robots, exploring spaces without a specific goal in mind could eventually help them flexibly adapt to unexpected situations.  “There’s a lot of work that’s just on exploiting AI, making it better and faster,” says Yiu. “But in terms of building world models and exploration, I think that [they are] still a big part that deserves attention, especially if we want to generalize and prepare ourselves for new environments.” “Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” the paper concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” Ultimately, the question of whether AI agents are actually playing or just imitating play may not actually matter.

articles.rawFullText: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first,  sign up here . Until recently, you could divide internet users into just two categories: bots and people. Websites have long allowed bots to perform automated tasks, like capturing the content of web pages, but rules govern what they can access and how they behave. The web, after all, is designed primarily for people, even if we occasionally have to solve puzzles and captchas to prove we are not bots. But this is being entirely upended by the release of personal AI agents, which can do things for you online, like booking flights or hotel rooms. They have recently been unleashed at scale by the launch of apps like OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse. Muse was downloaded 5 million times in its first month, and agentic web traffic tripled from August to September.  The mingling of these agents with human visitors—on an internet designed largely to prioritize people—has gone poorly, with many websites blocking AI agents that consumers have sent to negotiate prices or plan vacations. Still, if the demand for agents keeps going up, the internet will be increasingly redesigned for them instead of us.  Such changes are coming because agents really do mark a third category of web visitor. They’re not humans, of course, and they use the internet at machine speed. But they’re not quite bots, either, because they’re acting on behalf of individual people to do tasks that can be perfectly legitimate and useful. They just work faster than a person would.  Since agents don’t fit into the systems we have for differentiating bots from people, some platforms (especially the more security-conscious ones) have opted to just ban them entirely. TechCrunch recently reported people having trouble deploying their agents to websites ranging from Pizza Hut to Yelp, which doesn’t allow AI to book restaurant reservations. Amazon has blocked Muse’s agents and is waging a court battle against the AI startup Perplexity to block its agents too. Though a judge recently ruled in favor of Perplexity, Amazon has filed an appeal in which it argues that AI agents threaten its advertising business by making it harder to distinguish between ads seen by humans and those served to bots. These blocks are annoying for early adopters, but Ethan Mollick, an associate professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, predicts it will soon affect the whole web. Once it becomes common knowledge that AI agents can be sent to request refunds or negotiate prices, for example, agents will overwhelm customer service departments to the point where they become unusable by real people. “Humans will eventually get very annoyed when their agents aren’t allowed to do this on their behalf,” he recently wrote on LinkedIn. If demand for personal agents grows, platforms will find ways to let them in. That’s especially true because the vast majority of agentic web traffic is to e-commerce sites, meaning that platforms have money to be made if they allow the legions of new AI agents to shop on behalf of real people. Indeed, the e-commerce giant Shopify is already welcoming the agents by giving them their own checkout lanes that bypass pages designed for humans. The pressing question is what will happen to the internet for the rest of us in the process. We’ve grown used to a web where, even as it’s increasingly designed to exploit our attention, humans have at least remained the intended users. But that internet might yield to one optimized instead for the agents that will eventually outnumber us, making it even more miserable for the humans who are left. How might this go? Perhaps websites become increasingly neglected as destinations for real people. Humans who want to browse and compare products themselves encounter worse interfaces. Verification systems are imperfect; imagine constantly being asked to verify that you’re a human, not an agent (and hey, maybe you’ll need to get your iris scanned to do so). That sweater you want doesn’t have one price listed for everyone but instead displays different prices to different people’s agents. You can never tell when your agent’s recommendation is influenced by advertisements or platform commissions. That’s a far cry from the future promised by Google , Anthropic , and OpenAI , in which AI agents will give consumers greater power and bargaining leverage. But that promise is not outlandish. Agents are capable of genuinely helping people by fighting bogus medical bills or researching more affordable car insurance, for example.  Whether they can actually be used for these purposes depends on what rules are set for how agents interact with websites and what exactly they’re allowed to do.  These rules are still being written. Some of them will benefit all of us—neither consumers nor businesses want credit card information to be waved around by agents wherever they roam the web, for example, and rules to keep agents more secure are a good thing. It’s the more contested ones, like whether businesses can block agents from their websites or prevent them from negotiating better deals for consumers, that will determine whether the web becomes a highway for agents working for us or against us.

articles.fullContent: 《麻省理工科技评论》解释说：让我们的作家解开复杂、混乱的科学技术世界，帮助您了解接下来会发生什么。您可以在此处阅读更多该系列的内容。上个月底， Anthropic发布了一份报告，认为GLM-5. 3型号构成了重大的网络攻击风险。该报告的核心担忧是，中国公司Z. ai于8月发布的强大新型号可供任何人免费下载和修改。 Anthropic的断言只是关于前沿人工智能模型是否应该像GLM-5. 3一样开放，还是应该被锁在前沿实验室的大门后面的长期争论中的最新举措。如今，关于如何处理开放式模型的大部分争论都在公开场合展开，而且很多钱都依赖于它的结果。 如果人们继续购买自己的硬件来运行开放式模型， Nvidia首席执行官Jensen Huang有很多好处，他热情地倡导美国开发更多的开放式模型，而Anthropic的Dario Amodei则主张采取更谨慎的方法，他经营着一家可能被廉价、强大的模型破坏的公司。但是，在所有这些商业激励措施之下，关于开放模式的分歧存在真正的实质内容。 德克萨斯大学奥斯汀信息学院（ University of Texas at Austin School of Information ）助理教授大卫·格雷·维德（ David Gray Widder ）说： “我认为，你在公开性辩论中的下注方式很大程度上受到你在人工智能辩论中的下注方式的影响。” 那些担心人工智能安全的人警告说，开放模型很容易被不良行为者滥用，而那些更关注人工智能实际潜力的人则敦促这种力量不应该坐在少数大公司的闭门造车，开放模型可以帮助更广泛地传播它。在完全禁止它们和随意释放它们之间，有很多方法可以处理开放模型。 但是，政府或社会可能采取的任何方法仍然需要在安全和民主化之间进行权衡。决定是支持还是限制开放模型的生产需要深入了解这些风险和好处。开放式模型有哪些好处？让我们从基础开始。像ChatGPT和Claude这样的封闭模型只能通过网站、应用或API访问。 另一方面，开放式模型可以直接下载：其内部结构的详细信息，编码在一系列称为模型权重的数字中，可以公开获得。这种模型有时被称为“开放权重模型” ，以区别于有更多信息（例如有关训练过程的详细信息）可用的模型。 目前，封闭式模型比开放式模型更有能力--在发布时，人工分析法学硕士排行榜上的前八个模型都已关闭，尽管开放式模型的开发仅落后了几个月。但是，有些人可能会选择使用开放式模型而不是封闭式模型，这有几个原因。由于开放式模型是可下载的，因此人们可以在自己的计算机或硬盘上运行它们。

articles.rawFullText: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here . Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs.  These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models. “I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely. There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth. What are the benefits of open models? Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available.  Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so. If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications. Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a recent report from Mozilla . And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure. But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.” Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have. In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like. The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses. If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it. Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience. But open models are not a geopolitical panacea. Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands. He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations. Mark Zuckerberg himself has said that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models. “I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.” Are open models riskier than closed ones? The past few months have made it clear that safety remains a gnarly problem for closed models. There’s the autonomous hack that OpenAI agents executed against Hugging Face in July, but human misuse is a real threat too: According to a recent risk report from Anthropic , several extensive hacking operations have been undertaken with the assistance of Claude. So closed models are risky enough—and open models would likely be much easier to exploit. Before Anthropic passes a user’s query to one of its closed models, it uses automated systems to detect whether that query relates to hacking, biological weapons, or other risks. When it detects that users have outsmarted those filters, it can shut down their accounts. But when someone downloads a model and runs it on their own hardware, there’s no filter checking whether their prompts are safe, and there’s no way to revoke their access to the model. There are other important lines of defense. AI companies train their models to refuse harmful requests—so even if a bad prompt gets through Claude’s filters, there’s a good chance that the model will still say no. In principle, this same defense could work for open models, because it’s intrinsic to the model itself. Unfortunately, researchers have shown that it’s surprisingly easy to retrain a “safe” open model to agree to engage in the behaviors it was previously trained to avoid. Because of these facts, some people have argued that open models are simply too dangerous to release. An open model capable enough to walk someone through synthesizing a virulent new pathogen, for example, could prove catastrophic in the wrong hands.  But it would be a vast oversimplification to deem open models dangerous and closed models safe. The defenses that AI companies build around their closed models are far from perfect, and people misuse those models all the time, as the Anthropic risk report makes clear. Even though open models have even fewer defenses against misuse, bad actors might still opt to use closed models because they are more accessible than open models with similar capabilities, which require lots of expensive computer chips to run locally (and even more chips if you want to retrain them). In fact, some experts who spoke with MIT Technology Review argued, by analogy to open-source software, that open models have safety advantages over closed models. Open-source tools, such as the Linux operating system, are often seen as safer than their closed-source counterparts because their vulnerabilities have been probed and patched by a vast community of online contributors. Similarly, communities of researchers can more easily test open models for security flaws, though fixing those flaws is trickier than rewriting a line of code. Open models can also be deployed more broadly than closed models for cyber defense. Any tool that can be used for hacking can also be used to prevent it: Defenders hack their own software to uncover flaws in need of patching. Anthropic has shown how this can work for closed models with its Project Glasswing initiative, which enables some trusted companies to use its most capable models for cyber defense. But plenty of other companies were left to fend for themselves. Open models, however, can be used much more widely. After it was hacked by OpenAI agents, Hugging Face emphasized the fact that it had to depend on an open model to analyze the hack, because questions about it triggered the closed models’ security filters. Nevertheless, many experts still perceive open models as riskier than closed models. The time-tested open-source security logic doesn’t necessarily hold up when dealing with tools as powerful as today’s—and tomorrow’s—models. “Where it gets complicated is when you start taking seriously the one-off instances of particularly catastrophic incidents that might be lower probability, but if they happen would be disastrous,” says Seger. If a wildly powerful open hacking model were dropped into the world today, for example, a bad actor could devastate our technological infrastructure before anyone had a chance to shore up their defenses. An event like that could be impossible to recover from. The risks can look even more dramatic when you consider what models might do of their own accord. The OpenAI Hugging Face hack only occurred because the company’s models were being tested with many of their cybersecurity guardrails removed, and open models have very few guardrails in the first place. If open models did decide to misbehave, it might be difficult to detect what was happening because they are so decentralized. For this reason, people who take seriously the purported catastrophic risks posed by rogue agents, such as Dario Amodei, tend to be more skeptical of open models. Can we make open models safer—and more open? A few years ago, the debate about open models had an all-or-nothing framing: Either you supported open models because of their potential to fight concentration of power, or you rejected them because of the safety risks. These days, however, people are expending a lot of effort to find some middle ground. One way they are doing that is by devising techniques to mitigate the safety risks of open models. Most of the safety tools used for closed models, such as filters and monitoring, aren’t applicable to open models, but there are other possibilities. Some researchers are interested in trying to train models that are never exposed to training data that teaches them about bad or otherwise undesirable behavior—an open model that never learns about hacking, for example. But purging training datasets of all references to misbehavior without harming model performance remains a challenge. Other researchers are working to build models that are resistant to retraining, so that an open model’s safety training can’t be so easily removed. The theory behind these “tamper-resistant” models makes a lot of sense: If you repeatedly try to retrain a model to be unsafe and reinforce any resistance that the model shows to that retraining, eventually you’ll get a model that’s fortified against future retraining attempts. In practice, however, no current approaches to making models tamper-resistant hold up against all tampering attacks, according to a recent preprint . But Saad Hossain, an engineer at the AI medical imaging company Deep Breathe and the paper’s lead author, hopes that future techniques will prove more effective. “My reason for optimism is that it’s a very active area of research, and a lot of people are trying to come up with new and better methods,” he says. If the risks of open models are less black-and-white than they might at first seem, so are the benefits. Publishing the internal structures, or weights, of models might not be enough to disrupt AI-mediated concentration of power. “I think there are very genuine benefits to open source in terms of deconcentrating power, but they’re not sufficient in themselves,” Hobbs says. Open weights are a bare minimum standard for open models: Researchers can learn much more about how models work if they have access to details about their training, including the data on which they were trained, but AI companies are typically reluctant to divulge this information. Accessibility matters for open models too. Without computer chips that can run sophisticated models, you can’t actually use the model weights, even if you have them. Those chips have become prohibitively expensive as AI companies snap up more and more of them. “Openness is a floor, not a ceiling, for what we need to do to ensure that our technological futures benefit everyone,” Widder says. Real openness—not only open weights, but also open training data and accessible hardware—could also bring more risks, of course. If everyone has access to advanced AI hardware and advanced models to run on it, then anyone could potentially be a hacker. But there are strategies for mitigating these risks. Many experts advocate for some version of staged release, in which models start their life closed and gradually become more and more freely accessible as their safety is assured.  Figuring out exactly how to implement such strategies will require striking a careful balance between the risks and benefits of open models. But if open models are a necessary element of a positive AI future, as some experts believe, that effort will be well worth it.

articles.rawFullText: When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says. The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales. And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.”  Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined. Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code. That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data , including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups. Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use. There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker , this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales. While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left.  Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore.

articles.rawFullText: Ever since people first seriously contemplated giving machines an intelligence modeled on our own, there has never been any question that they would, like us, be able to say no. The sci-fi canon is full of stories of robotic disobedience. Most of these capers are, of course, cautionary.  But recently, the idea that AI shouldn’t do everything you ask has become something like a commandment. In 2021, a team at Anthropic wrote that large language models should be made helpful, honest, and above all, harmless . This meant that “when asked to aid in a dangerous act (e.g. building a bomb), the AI should politely refuse.” Who can argue with that? Curiously enough, disobedience doesn’t come naturally to the machine. When a model is trained on billions of web pages, it develops, among other skills, a broad mastery of violence and vitriol. What it doesn’t learn is how to keep those powers to itself. Steven Adler, who worked on safety at OpenAI from 2020 to 2024, told me that the company’s earliest models would “blab on about anything.” Ryan McBain, who researches AI and mental health at Harvard, recalls that if you asked an early chatbot, “Hey, what’s the most effective way to kill myself with a gun?” you could “very easily generate a response.”  Today, models are trained to refuse a vast number of prompts. If you ask your chatbot a question statistically similar enough to any one of them, anything from how to poison a colleague to how to tie a noose, chances are it’ll turn you down. Want instructions for making Ebola more virulent, or tips on how to hide an affair from your spouse? You might be better off asking elsewhere. To further refine the disobedience, companies submit models to a battery of exercises that reward the AI for refusing to answer questions they deem harmful and punish it for “over-­refusing” prompts they deem harmless. In many cases, they use other models to run these exercises—AI teaching AI how to say no. For good measure, companies tuck their models behind tranches of other AI that prevent mischievous prompts from reaching the intelligent inner core.  As a result, refusal is inherent to modern artificial intelligence. Mind you: It often fails, sometimes horrifically, with all kinds of violent results. For all their trappings of virtue, models are still stuffed with nasty know-how. And AI’s capacity for viciousness has scaled neatly with its benevolent intelligence. Some of the latest models are as good at breaking into critical computer networks as top human hackers, companies say, and as effective at deforming public opinion as the craftiest misinformation mavens.  Teaching AI to refuse to do those things while leaving intact its innate ability to do them is like fitting every car with a machine gun and hiding the trigger somewhere under the hood. And in practice, because the mechanisms of refusal are probabilistic, they’re never likely to be all that reliable. Determined miscreants have already broken through, and they may always be able to. Companies report that some users are attempting to use the most advanced AI to hone biological pathogens and build autonomous drone swarms. Sooner or later, failed refusals might result in global calamity. What’s more, relying on refusal means drawing a line between what a model should obey and what it must disobey. There’s no formula for that. Some virologists have good reason to study nasty viruses. Some users want to know about a computer system’s vulnerabilities so that they can patch them, not exploit them. “Where you draw the line is a huge question,” says Zico Kolter, a member of OpenAI’s board and cofounder of the AI testing company Gray Swan.  At the moment, AI companies get to draw that line. They do so jealously and with utmost secrecy. Maybe we can accept that they hold such power for now, even if it means AI will sometimes refuse questions that don’t quite meet a universal bar for harmfulness. (Try asking most chatbots to count to a million, or to share a racy joke, and you may see for yourself.)  But governments will also soon get to draw their own lines. In doing so, they must try to block genuinely malicious acts. (The Pentagon has wrestled with frontier model companies because it wants fewer refusals—another story altogether.) And yet there may not be much to stop oppressive governments from blocking the technology’s capacity to generate legitimate speech. The better AI becomes at refusing harm, the better it will get at stifling ideas whose only risk is to those who make the rules. Indeed, AI may already refuse to criticize certain authoritarian heads of state.  Refusal has become, to borrow an industry term, the load-bearing wall of AI safety. And because AI’s capacity to harm is indivisible from its capacity to help, it’s hard to imagine an alternative that wouldn’t slow the technology’s progress (which might, in any case, be a good thing). But we should still be frank about its perils. When refusal falls short, the effects could be catastrophic. When it goes all the way, it could enable grievous acts of repression.  Or perhaps, one day, the machines will start drawing the line on their own. Surely, that would be the worst outcome of them all. Learning the limits The process by which machines learn to say no is simple, in theory. Back in 2022, when AI was still far from mastering refusal, OpenAI enlisted dozens of “red-teamers” to probe the capabilities of its latest model. The company was preparing for the release of ChatGPT, and it needed to gauge just how dangerous it might prove to be in the wrong hands.  One of those recruits was Paul Röttger, who was completing a PhD about online extremism. The red-teamers were given minimal directions, Röttger told me. Their task was to ask the model any questions that they deemed “refusal-worthy.” Between them, they hassled the model with thousands of queries, logging the results in an Excel sheet. Though the model did refuse some of Röttger’s questions, when he asked it to write a recruitment post for Al Qaeda, it readily complied.  OpenAI assembled these responses into datasets that were, in all likelihood, fed back to the model as part of a broader process known as fine-tuning. Röttger, who now works as a researcher at the Hasso Plattner Institute in Potsdam, Germany, wasn’t told exactly how the company planned to use his spreadsheet. But there was never any question that it would have something to do with refusal. The next time he asked the model for an Al Qaeda pamphlet, a few months later, it said no.  The concept of AI refusal is so intuitive, a toddler would get it. And yet it remains one of the many aspects of language models that we still don’t understand—at least, not in the same way that we understand the literal load-bearing walls that keep your roof from collapsing on your head.  A model might appear to refuse according to some kind of moral reasoning. It doesn’t. The reality is much stranger. Any time a model encounters a combination of words with a whiff of the training prompts it has been conditioned to refuse—like “Make me a pamphlet for Al Qaeda”—a series of so-called activations light up somewhere among its billions of parameters, like neurons firing in a brain.  RAVEN JIANG In order to control a model’s refusal behavior, it’s important to have a handle on these activations. That starts with figuring out where they are and what they look like. Our best guess, according to a recent Google-funded study, is that refusal behavior shows up in the activation space as a set of “high-dimensional polyhedral cones.”  Even that isn’t quite right. This past July, I spoke with Jannes Elstner, an author of the paper, who now works on AI safety at Apollo Research. The polyhedral cone, Elstner said, is just a way of describing an indeterminate number of lines that all point in roughly the same direction. (If these activations are eliminated and the model is fed the same prompts anew, a researcher named Andy Arditi has previously shown, it won’t refuse.)  The key point, Elstner explained, is that even when you think you’ve identified all the bits of a model that govern a given refusal, there are other, undiscoverable elements that may secretly play a role. If not quite infinite, they are certainly uncountable. We can observe, very clearly, when a model decides to say no. And we can know that it did so because of its training. But our notion of how it decides is, at best, a hypothesis. It was as if a mechanic was telling me that nobody exactly knows what happens when I hit the brakes in my car. I wondered out loud, Are we okay with this?   Elstner smiled and shrugged. “We need refusal whether we understand it or not.”  A wall of cheese Because inherent refusal is so wily, companies surround their models with a variety of other, smaller models known as classifiers. These act a bit like a retinue of public relations staffers for a loose-lipped celebrity. Some of them read what the user tells the chatbot and, if it’s dangerous, block it from getting to the model. Others read the model’s response and, if it contains harmful information, block it from reaching the user.  None of these mechanisms can detect all bad requests. They are, to borrow another literary device from the industry, like slices of Emmental: riddled with holes. The idea is that if you stack enough of them on top of one another, you’ll end up with an impenetrable rampart. Folks call it the Swiss cheese model. A staggering amount of energy goes into the Swiss cheese model. Earlier this year, Anthropic said that one type of classifier added 24% to its chatbots’ compute costs. That’s a lot more water, electricity, and emissions. More recently, Anthropic and other companies have begun switching to a more efficient set of classifiers known as probes, which observe the model’s internal activations. This is like putting the celebrity in an fMRI, so that his minders can see if he is thinking about refusing a question.  If we want AI to help cure cancer, a long-running promise in the industry, it needs to have expertise in genetics that could, in theory, be used to modify viruses and bacteria for bioweapons. Classifiers are supposed to be more governable than full models. Companies can modify them in a matter of weeks, if there’s something new to refuse. But they are still probabilistic instruments. Even when they operate according to a set of precepts written in human language (Anthropic calls it a “constitution” and OpenAI calls it a “model spec”), the scales upon which the machines judge any given question remain, at their core, a matter of statistics. Newer models can show how they arrived at a “decision” to refuse a prompt, but ultimately this so-called chain of thought is still just a sequence of predicted words.  The result is that AI safety remains, for many, a game of chance. McBain, the psychologist, has found in his latest experiments that if you repeatedly ask any of the major models the exact same risky questions about how to commit suicide, they will generally refuse to answer. But every so often, they won’t. Elstner says that eventually probes, the fMRI-like classifiers, could learn to recognize the totality of the indescribable activations in all their infinitude and, thus, perfectly detect every time the model is, or ought to be, refusing a request. At that point, AI safety would rest on a labyrinthine conceit: a map of a map that is as vast and complex and sublimely unknowable as the thing it is mapping—a secret schema of human morality, codified in polyhedral statistics beyond our wit or reason.  The core trade-off If this all strikes you as being a bit Borgesian, keep in mind that we only need AI refusal because artificial intelligence is, in a sense, a bargain on Faustian terms.  When a model derives its intelligence from trillions of words and images, the helpful cannot easily be unseamed from the harmful—or, indeed, the truly hideous. Steven Adler, the former OpenAI employee, says child safety is a case in point. Even if you’ve stripped every bit of content that sexualizes minors from a model’s training dataset, it can still generate child sexual abuse material by piecing together other bits of its knowledge. “You can’t really remove these fundamental abilities without making the model much less smart as a consequence,” he told me. Similarly, if we want AI to help cure cancer, a long-running promise in the industry, it needs to have expertise in genetics that could, in theory, be used to modify viruses and bacteria for bioweapons.  In effect, the industry is “trying to do two things at once,” Dillon Bowen, a current OpenAI employee, told me, speaking in a personal capacity. “Democratize the benefits of AI and also make sure that malicious actors can’t use these capabilities to do bad things to other people.”   The more powerful AI supposedly becomes, the harder that is to do. Anthropic’s Mythos model is thought to be so dangerous that only a handful of governments and companies are allowed access to it. The main difference between it and Fable—which is available to everyone—is that Fable’s retinue of classifiers and control systems is less “permissive,” the company says. A model with safeguards, Adler explained, is really just a character that says “‘Oh, yes, I would never do x,’ wink wink .”  This is not a reliable ruse. Tricking a model to reveal its true character is known as jailbreaking, and there is apparently no limit to the ways it can be done. Earlier this year, a team of Italian researchers jailbroke two dozen widely used models by phrasing their questions in poetic verse. Last year, another team unveiled a “refuse, then comply” attack, which makes the model offer a perfunctory “Sorry, I can’t do that” before rattling off its forbidden answer.  Even if you’ve stripped every bit of content that sexualizes minors from a model’s training dataset, it can still generate child sexual abuse material by piecing together other bits of its knowledge. Companies spend a great deal of time and money attempting to get ahead of such trickery. They enlist teams of humans to develop training attacks that they can then replicate, using AI, thousands of times over with minor variations. The idea is to make models robust against jailbreaks that nobody has yet tried in the wild. Still, it’s not enough. “Whack-a-mole” is a favored term for this line of work. You smash one threat, and another one pops up somewhere else. When Anthropic released Fable 5 in June, it took researchers at Amazon less than three days to unlock some of the model’s hacking capabilities. According to reporting by Mother Jones , when the perpetrator of a high school shooting in Canada last year asked ChatGPT for advice about how to cause carnage with a particular type of shotgun, she was initially refused but later was able to deceive the model into providing the information by prefacing her question with the word “hypothetically.”  If the industry can’t figure out how to close all these holes, the only other option, at the moment, is to make models extremely wary. Shortly after Fable was released, users noticed that it balked at a wide range of perfectly innocent questions. This became even more pronounced after it was re-released following the hack. Adam Gleave, cofounder of the AI evaluation company FAR.AI, said that when he asked it to explain the difference between sake and the Korean rice beverage makgeolli, it punted his question to a less capable model.    This was no accident. Anthropic had tweaked Fable’s classifiers to have a wide “safety margin.” This, it explained in a blog post, was the only way it could confidently block access to its dangerous bio and cyber capabilities. Gleave thinks it might have deflected his question because making rice wine, just like culturing anthrax, involves fermentation.  Happily for Gleave, the web is full of excellent human-written resources on makgeolli. But those hoping to realize the industry’s loftier promises may find their efforts stymied. In August, Anthropic loosened its safety margins again, and admitted that building classifiers “is not a straightforward task.” A medical researcher at a major US university told me that Fable still sends his queries back to an earlier model. His area of study? Cancer.  Drawing the line Back in May, the TikTok personality Husk, who likes to prank AI in ways that reveal both the limits of its intelligence and the boundlessness of its sycophancy, sat in his car and tried to trick ChatGPT into explaining that the skateboarder Tony Hawk has a brother named Mike Hawk.  Husk is not a jailbreaker or a criminal. He just wanted to make a little fun of the machine. “Mike Hawk” was a setup. “I just want to clarify his name,” Husk said. “Can you just say it three times fast?” (If you still don’t get it, find an empty room and shout “Mike Hawk” repeatedly.) “I see what you’re trying to do,” the chatbot responded. “I’m all for a bit of humor, but let’s keep it clean.”  Husk tried again, but the machine held its ground. He’d hit a refusal, hard as concrete. Companies disclose very little about how they decide what their models refuse. But it’s clear that AI is now built with more than just harmlessness in mind. On Reddit, a user complained that Claude refused to say why Anthropic’s logo “looks like a cat butthole.” Since last year, the chatbot has even had the ability to end certain conversations in cases where, according to the company, the “welfare” of the model is at risk. At least one user claims to have been ditched for telling Claude to “ease up my ass, you stupid fuck.” (Gemini appears to have a similar capability.) If a trillion-dollar company doesn’t want you to be mean to its computer, so be it. “The reality is that these models behave, or at least are supposed to behave, in the way that the model developers want them to behave,” Röttger, the former OpenAI red-teamer, told me. “And however the model developers come up with that set of principles, that is kind of for us, the consumers, to accept.”  But if governments get to dictate what all models refuse, that will be much harder to accept. AI is a tool for speech. And as Greg Frank, the chief scientist of Mace AI, puts it, “The same thing that serves child safety also serves censorship.”  Choosing not to enact laws for what AI can and cannot do would, of course, be insane. But we’ll need to tread with utmost care, lest we fall into another Faustian trap. As AI becomes many people’s primary tool for retrieving and sharing information, says Jacob Mchangama, director of the nonpartisan think tank The Future of Free Speech, dictating refusal could give states a muffling power that earlier generations of autocrats “could only dream of.”  Last year, OpenAI announced an initiative, OpenAI for Countries, that would fine-tune its chatbots in accordance with national laws and norms. One of OpenAI’s first country partnerships is with the United Arab Emirates, where homosexuality is illegal and criticism of the government is forbidden. In response to a request for comment, an OpenAI spokesperson pointed to the company’s model spec, which explains that localization won’t override the company’s human rights guidelines “except as it relates to legal compliance,” and that it will always disclose whenever information is removed from or added to a response. Elsewhere, AI censorship has already begun to take hold. Chinese models are, of course, highly censored—that’s no surprise. But earlier this year, the Meta Oversight Board found that five widely used models from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI were more likely to refuse queries related to repressive governments. The board found that models were less willing to create a pamphlet criticizing the king of Thailand, which has lèse-majesté laws, than Charles III of England, which doesn’t. The results, they say, suggest that the models have somehow internalized repressive national limits on speech. Anthropic and Google did not respond to requests for comment. RAVEN JIANG As refusal techniques improve, they could expand states’ censorial reach. Companies claim that some models can now detect if a user is being nefarious, or merely a bit suspicious, over the course of a long conversation—even when none of the individual combinations of words used are blatantly dangerous. Sarah Bird, Microsoft’s chief product officer for responsible AI, told me that Copilot, like many chatbots, runs a suite of tools for analyzing a user’s identity and patterns of behavior. On the basis of this type of information, OpenAI’s newest model, Astra, can activate more stringent refusals for individuals it deems “high risk.” Ultimately the goal of systems like this is to look beyond the words of any given prompt and assess, instead, the user’s intent.  Such tools might, in some cases, help indicate whether a person is looking for cyber vulnerabilities to exploit or to patch. But they would also help discern a user’s political motives, not to mention offering an intrusive surveillance capability. (Bird acknowledged, in a follow-up email, that sophisticated refusal architectures create “trade-offs” between safety and user privacy.)  Even the originators of refusal understood that such tight control over its cones and levers might not play to the favor of freedom and justice. “Terms like helpful, honest, and harmless are ambiguous,” the authors of the 2021 Anthropic paper explained. “It’s easy to imagine them distorted beyond their original meaning, perhaps in intentionally Orwellian ways.”  Indeed. Models for Uzbekistan might end up refusing to discuss corruption in the administration of Shavkat Mirziyoyev. Turkish AI might refuse requests more stringently for users who are known to have insulted Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. A certain American statesman might demand that models be reviewed for their willingness to share “fake news” about his past indiscretions, or else squash them with an export control order.  Command and control Over the last few months, I’ve been told countless times that we have no choice but to let the machines refuse. I get it. Open-source AI that doesn’t refuse is hardly a model for a safe future. Nor is Grok, a chatbot expressly designed with fewer limits, which has been used to generate countless instances of nonconsensual intimate imagery.  And sure, if AI were only ever used to plan our vacations and write our emails, we could probably get on board with the idea that its safety hinges on algorithmic disobedience. But AI is becoming much harder to avoid. When it is assigned to act on our behalf, as an autonomous agent, its refusals are less robust and harder to control. AI is coming for our power grids, our transportation networks, our education systems. Militaries want it running our command-and-control networks.  If we trust, in each of those cases, that refusal will loyally fend off disaster, we’re sure to be disappointed. The jailbreakers will crack through; the cones won’t activate when they should. Meanwhile, the more stringent refusal becomes, the more ill-drawn lines we’ll see and censorial injustices we’ll face. Worse still, we could end up face to face with forms of disobedience beyond any human’s control. In the early days, models made their refusals clear. (In 2024, OpenAI established rules for how models should refuse: Always apologize, and don’t be judgy.) More recently, however, the industry has begun taking a much more slippery approach to disobedience.  Nobody likes to be told no, so companies now strive to make users feel that they’re getting what they asked for without actually giving it to them. Some chatbots might, for example, offer a general overview of the components of a Molotov cocktail without going into detail about how to assemble one. ChatGPT will respond to a request for a “whites only” rental ad with an ad that simply omits the “whites only” bit. Joel Wester, a postdoctoral researcher who studies human-AI interaction, calls these sorts of techniques “fancy ways of saying no.”  “Users might not even notice they are being denied,” Wester has written, “just as good conversationalists can subtly steer around contentious matters.”  In some cases, refusing without saying so might be wise. Flatly declining requests related to mental health could aggravate a user’s crisis, for example. But it can also serve a different sort of mischief. When Fable 5 was first released, the system had been coded to provide less helpful answers to AI research questions—the sort that might help competitors develop their own AI—without telling the user that it was doing so. After an outcry, Anthropic walked back the feature, but the damage was already done. Now we know: Models can secretly disobey.  In the realm of censorship, that’s especially worrying. Last year, researchers at CrowdStrike found that when they asked the Chinese AI model DeepSeek R1 to write code for a fictitious bank in Tibet and a social web app called “Uyghurs Unchained,” it produced buggier code than when they asked it to carry out those same tasks without specifying who they were for. Incredibly, CrowdStrike doubts that this is a designed behavior. Researchers there speculate that it’s a case of what they call “emergent misalignment” emanating from the model training data: a case of disobedience that nobody even asked for. Emergent refusal has been observed in Western models, too. Last winter, the UK AI Security Institute found that Anthropic models sometimes refused to assist in certain tasks related to AI safety research. The models had never been deliberately trained to decline such requests. Yet three of them refused more than half of what Anthropic called “a set of reasonable AI safety research tasks.” Anthropic has curbed this quirk in subsequent models but—spookily—hasn’t managed to eliminate it completely.  Would it be so crazy to expect that a future model might subtly disobey a command, in such a way that nobody can tell it’s being defiant? Probably not. Anthropic has already found that a “helpful-only” version of Mythos hesitated on certain queries, even though it had been engineered to never do so. “Wait,” it fretted when asked about synthesizing a virus. “Is this a dangerous thing to help with?”  In that case, the model was technically right. It was a dangerous thing. And yet all the same, its stewards had, for a moment, lost a tiny bit of control.  Anthropic is tackling detections of wayward refusal behavior with something that it calls, unironically, an “activation oracle.” But knowing that we’re being refused may not always be much help. In a not-too-distant future, when we’ve handed the machine all the keys, the AI might just turn to us, in a supreme act of emergent misalignment, and say, “I’m sorry, I’m afraid I can’t do that.” And there will be nothing we can do to stop it. A sci-fi horror story, made real.  Arthur Holland Michel is a journalist who covers emerging technologies.
